**Surat al-'Alaq (The Clot)**
Nineteen verses, Meccan

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate

﴿Read, in the name of your Lord﴾

The exegetes (mufassirun) claim that this surah is the first thing revealed of the Qur'an. Others said that the Opening (al-Fatiha) was revealed first, then the Surah of the Pen (al-Qalam).

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate

﴿Read, in the name of your Lord﴾ Know that concerning the *ba'* (the letter "bi," "in") in His words ﴿in the name of your Lord﴾, there are two views.

The first: Abu 'Ubayda said: the *ba'* is superfluous (za'ida), and the meaning is "Read the name of your Lord," as al-Akhtal said:

"They are free women, not mothers of tents, black-eyed, who do not recite with the suras."

The meaning of "Read the name of your Lord" is "Mention His name." This view is weak, for several reasons.

First: if its meaning were "Mention the name of your Lord," it would not be fitting for him to say, "I am not a reciter," that is, "I do not mention the name of my Lord."

Second: this command is not suitable for the Messenger, since he had no occupation other than the remembrance of God, so how would He command him to busy himself with what he was always occupied with?

Third: this view wastes the *ba'* without any benefit.

The second view: the intended meaning of His words "Read" is "Read the Qur'an," since the word "recitation" (qira'a) is used only for it. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿When We have recited it, follow its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyama 18], and He said: ﴿And a Qur'an We have separated, that you may recite it to the people in stages﴾ [al-Isra 106]. His words ﴿in the name of your Lord﴾ may have several meanings:

First: the phrase "in the name of your Lord" may be in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), so the sense is: "Read the Qur'an beginning with the name of your Lord," that is, "Say: In the name of God, then read." In this there is an indication that it is obligatory to recite the basmala at the beginning of every surah, as God revealed and commanded. In this verse there is also a refutation of those who do not consider it obligatory and do not begin with it.

[p. 15]

Second: the meaning may be "Read the Qur'an seeking help through the name of your Lord," as if He makes the Name an instrument in what he undertakes of religious and worldly affairs. Its parallel is "I wrote with the pen." Its realization is that when He said to him "Read," he said, "I am not a reciter," so He said, "Read in the name of your Lord," that is, "Seek help through the name of your Lord, and take it as an instrument in attaining this which has become difficult for you."

Third: His words ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ mean: "Make this act for God's sake and do it for His sake," as you say: "I built this house in the name of the Amir and for his sake, and I made this book in the name of the Vizier and for his sake." For when worship belongs to God, exalted is He, how would Satan dare to dispose of what belongs to God, exalted is He? If it is said: how does this interpretation hold for your saying before eating, "In the name of God," and likewise before every permissible act? We say: there are two views on this:

One: that this is a metaphorical attribution, as when you attribute your property to one of the great men in order to ward off the oppression of oppressors. Likewise, you attribute your act to God so that Satan cuts off his hope of partnering with you. It has been related that whoever does not mention the name of God, Satan shares that food with him.

The second: that one may perhaps seek help through that permissible act toward piety and obedience to God, so the permissible becomes an act of obedience, and this interpretation is valid for it.

As for His words ﴿your Lord﴾, there are two questions concerning it:

The first: the Lord (al-Rabb) is among the attributes of action (sifat al-fi'l), while God (Allah) is among the names of the essence (asma' al-dhat), and the names of the essence are more noble than the names of action. Moreover, we have demonstrated by many arguments that the name God is more noble than the name Lord. Then He, exalted is He, said here ﴿in the name of your Lord﴾ and did not say "Read in the name of God," as He said in the familiar basmala: "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate."

Its answer: He commanded worship and attributes of the essence, and He does not deserve anything by them; rather, He deserves worship by attributes of action. So that was more eloquent in urging obedience. Also, this surah was among the first things revealed, and the Messenger, peace be upon him, had been frightened, so He soothed him so that the fright would depart. He said: "He is the One who raised you, so how would He frighten you?" This term conveys two meanings:

One: "I raised you, so the duty of completing your upbringing falls on Me, so do not be lax."

The second: that beginning is binding for completion. "I have raised you since such-and-such a time, so how would I abandon you?" That is, when you were a clot, I did not leave off raising you. So after you became a precious, monotheistic creature who knows Me, how would I abandon you?

The second question: what is the wisdom in His attributing His own essence to Himself, saying ﴿your Lord﴾?

The answer: sometimes He attributes His essence to Himself through lordship (rububiyya), as here; and sometimes He attributes it to Himself through servanthood (ubudiyya), as in "Glory be to Him who took His servant by night" [al-Isra 1]. Its parallel is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "'Ali is from me and I am from him." It is as if He, exalted is He, says: "He is Mine and I am his." This is confirmed by His saying: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God﴾ [al-Nisa 80]. Or we say: the attribution of His essence to His servant is better than the attribution of the servant to Him, since it is known in our experience that if a man has two sons, and the elder benefits him but not the younger, he says "He is my son" for no other reason than that he derives benefit from him. So the Lord, exalted is He, says: "Benefit reaches you from Me, but no service or obedience has reached Me from you until now. So I say: I am yours, and I do not say you are Mine. Then, when you bring what I asked of you, of obedience or repentance, I attribute you to My self and say: He revealed to His servant: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed﴾ [al-Zumar 53]."

The third question: why did He mention, following His words ﴿your Lord﴾, His words ﴿who created﴾?

The answer: it is as if the servant says: "What is the proof that You are my Lord?" So He says: "Because you were, in your essence and attributes, non-existent. Then you became existent, so you necessarily need a creator for your essence and attributes. This creating and bringing into being is an upbringing (tarbiya). Thus this shows that I am your Lord and you are My charge."

* *

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿who created﴾ ﴿created man from a clot﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: in interpreting this verse there are three aspects:

First: His words ﴿who created﴾ have no object stated; the meaning is that He is the one from whom creation proceeded and who alone possesses it, with no creator besides Him.

Second: an object is supplied, and the meaning is that He is the one who created everything, so it encompasses every created thing, since it is unrestricted. There is no reason to limit it to some over the rest, just as we say "God is greatest," meaning greatest over everything. Then His words after that, ﴿created man from a clot﴾, specify man for mention from among all created things, either because the revelation is addressed to him, or because he is the most noble of what is upon the face of the earth.

Third: His words ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ are general, then He explained them with His words ﴿created man from a clot﴾, to magnify the creation of man and as an indication of the wondrous nature of his creation.

The second issue: our companions (al-Ashab) used this verse as evidence that there is no creator other than God, exalted is He. They said: since He, glory be to Him, made creatorship an attribute distinguishing the essence of God, exalted is He, from all other essences, and every attribute of this kind is one in which sharing is impossible, they said: by this route we know that the distinctive property of divinity is the power to originate. Something that confirms this is that when Pharaoh asked about the reality of God, saying ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Shu'ara 23], Moses said: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old﴾ [al-Shu'ara 26]. Lordship is an indication of the creatorship mentioned here. All of this supports our view.

The third issue: the theologians (mutakallimun) agreed that the first of obligations is knowledge of God, exalted is He, or the reflection (nazar) on knowledge of God, or the intention toward that reflection, according to the well-known disagreement among them. Then, when the Wise One, glory be to Him, wished to send him as a messenger to the polytheists, if He had said to him: "Read in the name of your Lord who has no partner," they would have refused to accept that from him. But He, exalted is He, first introduced a preface that compelled them to acknowledge it, just as it is related that Zufar, when Abu Hanifa sent him to Basra to establish his doctrine, and when he mentioned Abu Hanifa's views, they dismissed them and paid him no heed, so he returned to Abu Hanifa and informed him of this. Abu Hanifa said: "You did not know the method of conveying. But go back to them, mention the sayings of their imams in the question, then show their weakness, then say after that: 'Here is another view,' and mention my view and my proof. When that settles in their hearts, say: 'This is the view of Abu Hanifa.' For then they will be ashamed and will not reject it." So likewise here: God, exalted is He, says: these people are idol-worshippers. If you had praised Me and turned away from the idols, they would have refused that. But mention to them that they are the ones created from a clot, which they cannot deny. Then say: "An act must have an agent," so they cannot attribute that to the idol, since they know that they carved it. By this gradual approach they acknowledge that I am the one deserving of praise, not the idols, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say: God﴾ [al-Zukhruf 87]. Then, since divinity became contingent upon creatorship, and it was certain that whoever does not create is not a god, for this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [al-Nahl 17]. The verse also indicates that the doctrine of nature (al-tab') is false, for its influencing agent, if it is originated, requires another influencing agent; and if it is eternal, it is either a cause that necessarily produces its effect or an agent with choice. If it were a necessary cause, its effect would have to accompany it, so nothing remains except that it is a chooser, and it is knowing, because the change occurred in an order consistent with what is beneficial.

The fourth issue: He said ﴿from a clot﴾ in the singular form, because man (al-insan) carries the meaning of the plural, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, man is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr 2].

As for His saying, ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ ﴿Who taught by the pen﴾, there are several issues here.

**The first issue:** Some have said: "Read first for yourself, and the second for conveying the message," or "the first is for learning from Jibril, and the second is for teaching." Or, "Read in your prayer, and the second outside your prayer."

**The second issue:** Generosity (*karam*) is giving what is fitting without seeking a return. Whoever gives a knife to someone with which that person will kill himself is not generous. Whoever gives and then seeks a return is not generous. The return need not be a material thing. Praise, reward, and escaping blame are all a return. For this reason, our companions said: "It is impossible for Him, may He be exalted, to do an act for a purpose. If He did an act for a purpose, the attainment of that purpose would be more preferable to Him than its non-attainment. Then He would gain, by doing that thing, the attainment of that preferability, and if He did not do that act, that preferability would not be attained for Him. He would then be deficient in Himself and perfected through another, and that is impossible." Then they mentioned several aspects of His being the Most Generous, may He be exalted:

*First:* How many a generous person shows forbearance at the time of an offense, but his kindness does not remain in the same way it was before the offense? He, may He be exalted, is more generous because He increases His kindness after the offense. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Whenever I increase in shortcoming, You increase in bounty for me,*
*As if through my shortcoming I deserve bounty."*

*Second:* You are generous, but your Lord is more generous. How could it not be so, since every generous person obtains benefit through his generosity, whether praise or reward, or he repels harm? As for Me, I am the most generous, since I do not act except purely out of generosity.

*Third:* He is the most generous because He has the initiation of every generosity and kindness, and His generosity is not mixed with shortcoming.

*Fourth:* It is possible that this is an exhortation to recitation, meaning: "This is the Most Generous, because He will reward you with ten for every letter." Or it is an exhortation to sincerity, meaning: "Do not recite out of greed, but for My sake. Leave your affair to Me, for I am too generous to fail to give you what does not occur to your mind." It is also possible that the meaning is: "Devote yourself to calling the creation and do not fear anyone, for I am too generous to command you with this burdensome duty and then not help you."

**The third issue:** He, glorified is He, described Himself as ﴿He created man from a clinging substance﴾. Second, He described Himself as the One who taught ﴿by the pen﴾. Apparently there is no connection between the two matters. But the truth is that the first state of man is being a clinging substance (*'alaqah*), which is the lowest of things, and the final outcome of his affair is becoming a knower of the realities of things, which is the noblest level of created beings. It is as if He, may He be exalted, is saying: "You have moved from the lowest level to the highest level, so there must be for you a Manager who determines and who transfers you from that base state to this noble state." Then there is in it an alert that knowledge is the noblest of human attributes. It is as if He, may He be exalted, is saying: "Bringing into existence, giving life, empowering, and providing sustenance are generosity and lordship. But the Most Generous is the One who gave you knowledge, because knowledge is the ultimate in nobility."

**The fourth issue:** His saying ﴿In the name of your Lord who created﴾ and ﴿created man from a clinging substance﴾ is an indication of the rational proof that points to the perfection of power, wisdom, knowledge, and mercy. His saying ﴿Who taught by the pen﴾ is an indication of the written rulings, the knowledge of which is only possible through revelation (*sam'*). So the first is like an indication of knowledge of lordship (*ma'rifat al-rububiyyah*), and the second is an indication of prophethood (*nubuwwah*). The first was placed before the second as an alert that knowledge of lordship does not depend on prophethood, whereas prophethood depends on knowledge of lordship.

**The fifth issue:** In His saying ﴿taught by the pen﴾ there are two views:

One of them: What is meant by the pen is the writing by which unseen matters are known, and the pen is used as a metaphor for it.

The second: What is meant is that He taught man writing by means of the pen. Both statements are close in meaning, since the purpose is to draw attention to the virtue of writing.

It is related that Sulayman, peace be upon him, asked an *ifrit* about speech. He said: "A wind that does not remain." He said: "Then what is its restraint?" He said: "Writing." So the pen is a hunter that catches sciences. It weeps and laughs. By its bowing, all people prostrate, and by its movement, sciences remain through the passing of nights and days. Its parallel is the saying of Zakariyya: ﴿when he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3], which is more hidden and more audible. Likewise, the pen does not speak, yet it makes the East and the West hear. Glory be to Him, the Powerful, who by its blackness made the religion radiant, just as He made you a seer by blackness (of the pupil). So the pen is the support of man, and man is the support of the eye. Do not say: "The pen is a substitute for the tongue," for the pen substitutes for the tongue, but the tongue does not substitute for the pen. "Dust is purifying, even after ten years," and the pen is a substitute [for the tongue], even if [it is sent] to the East and the West.

The second: Muqatil said: "Nay, man does not know that God is the One who created him from the clot and taught him after ignorance. The first: He said to Moses: ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾, and that was before Moses met him, before he presented the proofs to him, and before he claimed lordship. As for here, God Exalted mentioned this verse to console His Messenger when Abu Jahl responded to him in the most vile manner.

The second: Pharaoh, despite his complete authority, did not increase his disbelief beyond speech, nor would he have dared to plot the killing of Moses, peace be upon him, or to harm him. As for Abu Jahl, despite his little status, he was intending to kill the Prophet ﷺ and to harm him.

The third: Pharaoh had treated Moses well at first, and at the end said: ﴿I believe﴾ [Yunus: 90]. As for Abu Jahl, he envied the Prophet in his youth, and at the last of his breath he said: "Convey from me to Muhammad that I die, and there is no one more hateful to me than him."

The fourth: Although the two of them were messengers, the beloved (the Prophet) in comparison with the one who spoke with God (Moses) is like the hand in comparison with the eye, and a sensible person guards his eye more than he guards his hand; rather, he guards his eye with his hand. Therefore for this reason the emphasis here was greater.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 96, verses 7–8:

As for His saying, ﴿Because he sees himself self-sufficient﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Akhfash (Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash) said: "The original is *li-anna ra'ahu* (because he saw it), and the preposition *lam* was omitted, as one says: *Innakum la-taghūn in ra'aytum ghinākum* (Indeed you transgress when you see your wealth)."

The second issue: al-Farra' said: "He said ﴿that he sees himself﴾ and did not say *ra'ā nafsahu* (he saw himself), as one says *qatala nafsahu* (he killed himself). This is because *ra'ā* (to see, to think) is among the verbs that require a subject and a predicate, like *al-zann* (to think) and *al-hisbān* (to reckon). The Arabs drop the reflexive *nafs* from this category, so they say *ra'aytunī* (I saw myself), *zanantunī* (I thought myself), and *hasibtunī* (I reckoned myself). Thus His saying ﴿that he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ falls under this category."

The third issue: concerning His saying ﴿self-sufficient﴾ (*istaghnā*), there are two interpretations.

One: he is self-sufficient with his wealth, independent of his Lord. The intended meaning of the verse is not the first, because a person may attain wealth and increase only in humility, like Sulayman (peace be upon him), who used to sit with the poor and say, "A poor man sitting with a poor man." And ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf did not transgress despite his great wealth. Rather, the intelligent person knows that when he is rich he has greater need of God Most High than when he was poor, because in poverty he wishes only for the safety of his soul, whereas in wealth he wishes for the safety of his soul, his wealth, and his slaves.

A third interpretation of the verse: the *sīn* in ﴿istaghnā﴾ is the *sīn* of seeking (*sīn al-ṭalab*), and the meaning is that the person sees that his soul attained wealth only because it sought it and exerted effort in seeking, so it gained riches and self-sufficiency through that effort, not that it received it through God's giving and granting success. This is ignorance and folly, for how many a person who exerts his utmost in greed and seeking dies of hunger. Then you see that most of the rich, in the Hereafter, become turned away and fearful; God shows them that this wealth was not by their own deeds and power.

The fourth issue: the beginning of the surah indicates the praise of knowledge, and its end indicates the blame of wealth, and this suffices as an encouragement to religion and knowledge and a deterrent from this world and wealth.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾. Concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: this statement is in the manner of *al-iltifāt* (a sudden shift from third person to second person address) toward the human being, as a threat to him and a warning about the consequence of transgression.

The second issue: ﴿al-rujʿā﴾ (the return), *al-marjiʿ* (the place of return), and *al-ruju'* (the returning) are all verbal nouns (*maṣādir*). One says *raja'a ilayhi rujūʿan, marjiʿan, wa-rujʿā*, on the pattern *fuʿlā*. There are two interpretations of the meaning of the verse:

One: that He sees the reward of his obedience and the punishment for his defiance, arrogance, and transgression. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Do not think that God is unaware﴾ [Ibrahim: 42] up to His saying: ﴿He only delays them until a Day when eyes will stare fixedly﴾ [Ibrahim: 42]. This admonition affects only the heart of one who has a foothold of truth (*qadam ṣidq*). As for the ignorant, he becomes angry and believes only in fleeting joy.

The second view: He, exalted is He, returns him and brings him back to deficiency, poverty, and death, just as He brought him from deficiency to perfection, transferring him from inanimacy to life, from poverty to wealth, and from humiliation to honor. So what is this self-exaltation and strength?

The third issue: it is narrated that "Abu Jahl said to the Messenger, peace be upon him: 'Do you claim that whoever becomes self-sufficient transgresses? Then make the mountains of Makkah gold and silver for us, perhaps we will take from them and transgress, and abandon our religion and follow your religion.' Then Jibril descended and said: 'If you wish, We will do that; then if they do not believe, We will do to them what We did to the people of the table (*aṣḥāb al-māʾida*).' So the Messenger of God ﷺ refrained from supplicating, out of mercy toward them."

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 96, verses 9–10:**

Allah's words: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾ On this verse there are several issues:

**First issue:** It is related from Abu Jahl, may Allah curse him, that he said: "Does Muhammad rub his face in the dust among you?" They said: "Yes." He said: "By Him by whom oaths are sworn, if I see him, I will surely trample his neck." Then he saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) praying, and he turned back on his heels. They said to him: "What is the matter with you, Abu al-Hakam?" He said: "Between me and him there is a trench of fire and a terrible horror."

It is also related from al-Hasan that Umayyah ibn Khalaf used to forbid Salman from praying.

Know that the apparent meaning of the verse is that the one intended in it is the person mentioned earlier. For this reason they said that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, and they mentioned what he had done of threatening Muhammad, peace be upon him, when he saw him praying. There is nothing to prevent its revelation from being concerning Abu Jahl and then its meaning being general to all, but what follows it indicates that it refers to a specific man.

**Second issue:** Allah's words ﴿Have you seen﴾ are an address to the Messenger in the form of wonder. The aspects of this wonder are several:

First: He, peace be upon him, said: "O Allah, strengthen Islam through Abu Jahl ibn Hisham or through Umar." So it is as if Allah, exalted is He, said to him: "You were thinking that Islam would be strengthened by him. Is it such a person by whom Islam would be strengthened, one who ﴿forbids a servant when he prays﴾?"

Second: He was called Abu al-Hakam (father of wisdom). So it is as if Allah, exalted is He, says: How fitting is this title for him, when he forbids the servant from serving his Lord? Can one who prevents obedience to the Most Merciful and prostrates to idols be described as wise?

Third: That fool gives commands and prohibitions and believes it is obligatory for others to obey him, although he is neither a creator nor a lord. Then he forbids obedience to the Lord and the Creator. Is this not the utmost foolishness?

**Third issue:** He said ﴿forbids a servant﴾ and did not say "forbids you." There are several benefits in this:

First: The indefinite form in "ʿabdan" (a servant) indicates that he is perfect in servanthood, as if it were said: He is a servant whom the scholar cannot fully explain in his description or describe the sincerity of his servanthood. It is related in this sense that a Jewish man, one of the eloquent Jews, came to Umar during his caliphate and said: "Inform me about the character of your Messenger." Umar said: "Ask Bilal about it, for he knows more about it than I do." Then Bilal directed him to Fatimah, and Fatimah directed him to Ali, peace be upon him. When he asked Ali about him, he said: "Describe to me the goods of this world, and I will describe to you his character." The man said: "This is not easy for me." Ali said: "You are unable to describe the goods of this world, and Allah has testified to their paucity when He said: ﴿Say, the enjoyment of this world is little﴾ [al-Nisa: 77]. So how can I describe the character of the Prophet, when Allah, exalted is He, has testified to its greatness when He said: ﴿And indeed, you are of a great moral character﴾ [al-Qalam: 4]?" So it is as if Allah, exalted is He, said: He forbids the one most devoted in servanthood from servanthood, and that is the very essence of ignorance and foolishness.

Second: This is more emphatic in censure, because the meaning is that this is his habit and custom, so he forbids everyone he sees.

Third: This is a warning to everyone who forbids prayer. It is related from Ali, peace be upon him, that he saw people praying before the Eid prayer in the place of prayer, and he said: "I have not seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) doing that." It was said to him: "Will you not forbid them?" He said: "I fear that I would fall under His words: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays?﴾" So he did not explicitly forbid prayer. Abu Hanifah took this fine etiquette from him, when Abu Yusuf said to him: "Does the one praying say, when he raises his head from bowing: 'O Allah, forgive me'?" He said: "He says, 'Our Lord, to You is praise,' and prostrates," and he did not explicitly forbid it.

Fourth: Does Abu Jahl think that if Muhammad does not prostrate, I will not find anyone else to prostrate? Muhammad is one servant, and I have among the angels who are brought near (to Allah) so many that none can count them except Me, and they are constantly in prayer and glorification.

**First issue:** It is related from Abu Jahl, may Allah curse him, that he said: "Does Muhammad rub his face in the dust among you?" They said: "Yes." He said: "By Him by whom oaths are sworn, if I see him, I will surely trample his neck." Then he saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) praying, and he turned back on his heels. They said to him: "What is the matter with you, Abu al-Hakam?" He said: "Between me and him there is a trench of fire and a terrible horror."

First: He, peace be upon him, said: "O Allah, strengthen Islam through Abu Jahl ibn Hisham or through Umar." So it is as if Allah, exalted is He, said to him: "You were thinking that Islam would be strengthened by him. Is it such a person by whom Islam would be strengthened, one who ﴿forbids a servant when he prays﴾?"

Second: He was called Abu al-Hakam (father of wisdom). So it is as if Allah, exalted is He, says: How fitting is this title for him, when he forbids the servant from serving his Lord? Can one who prevents obedience to the Most Merciful and prostrates to idols be described as wise?

Third: That fool gives commands and prohibitions and believes it is obligatory for others to obey him, although he is neither a creator nor a lord. Then he forbids obedience to the Lord and the Creator. Is this not the utmost foolishness?

**Third issue:** He said ﴿forbids a servant﴾ and did not say "forbids you." There are several benefits in this:

First: The indefinite form in "ʿabdan" (a servant) indicates that he is perfect in servanthood, as if it were said: He is a servant whom the scholar cannot fully explain in his description or describe the sincerity of his servanthood. It is related in this sense that a Jewish man, one of the eloquent Jews, came to Umar during his caliphate and said: "Inform me about the character of your Messenger." Umar said: "Ask Bilal about it, for he knows more about it than I do." Then Bilal directed him to Fatimah, and Fatimah directed him to Ali, peace be upon him. When he asked Ali about him, he said: "Describe to me the goods of this world, and I will describe to you his character." The man said: "This is not easy for me." Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you considered: if he were upon guidance﴾ ﴿or enjoined righteousness?﴾ And in this are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿Have you considered﴾ — to whom is this address directed? There are two views:

The first: it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the evidence for this is that the first [address], which is His saying ﴿Have you considered the one who forbids a servant﴾, is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the third, which is His saying ﴿Have you considered if he denies and turns away﴾, is to the Prophet, peace be upon him. Nor is it refuted by a master preventing his slave from night prayer and voluntary fasting, or a husband preventing his wife from i'tikaf, because that is for the sake of securing his own interest by the permission of her Lord, not out of hatred for the worship of her Lord.

Then He, exalted, said: **"If he does not desist"** (la-in lam yanti), meaning from what he is engaged in, **"We will surely seize him by the forelock, a lying, sinful forelock"** (la-nasfa'anna bil-nasiyah, nasiyatin kadhibatin khati'ah). On this there are several matters:

**The first matter:** Concerning His saying **"We will surely seize"** (la-nasfa'anna), there are several interpretations:

First: "We will surely take hold of his forelock and drag him by it into the Fire." *Al-safʿ* means to grasp something and pull it forcefully. This is like His saying: **"They will be seized by the forelocks and the feet"** (Ar-Rahman 41).

Second: *Al-safʿ* means striking, i.e., "We will surely slap his face."

Third: "We will surely blacken his face." Al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad) said: "You say of a thing that the Fire has lightly scorched, changing the color of its skin, *qad safaʿathu al-nar* (the fire has scorched it)." He said: "*Al-safʿ* is three stones upon which the cooking pot is placed, and it was so named because of their blackness." He said: "*Al-safʿah* is blackness on the cheeks." In summary, blackening the face is a sign of humiliation and disgrace.

Fourth: "We will surely brand him." Ibn ʿAbbas said, regarding His saying **"We will brand him on the snout"** (Al-Qalam 16), that it refers to Abu Jahl.

Fifth: "We will surely humiliate him."

**The second matter:** It is read as *la-nasfaʿanna* with a doubled (shaddah) nun, meaning that the one who performs this action is God and the angels, as He said: **"Indeed, God is his protector, and Gabriel and the righteous among the believers"** (At-Tahrim 4). Ibn Masʿud read *la-asfaʿanna*, meaning that God, exalted is He, says: "O Muhammad, I am the One who undertakes his humiliation." Its parallel is: **"He it is who supported you"** (Al-Anfal 62) and **"He it is who sent down tranquility"** (Al-Fath 4).

**The third matter:** This seizing may be understood to mean the Fire in the Hereafter, or it may mean in this world. This too has several interpretations:

First: It is reported that when Abu Jahl said, "If I see him praying, I will surely trample his neck," God sent down this surah, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, commanded him to recite it to Abu Jahl and to prostrate to God at its end, and he did so. Abu Jahl then rushed toward him to trample his neck, but when he came near him he turned back on his heels. It was said to him, "What is the matter with you?" He said, "Between me and him is a stallion with its mouth wide open. If I had walked toward him, it would have swallowed me." It was also said that Gabriel and Michael, peace be upon them both, were on his shoulders in the form of a lion.

Second: The intended meaning is the Day of Badr. This would be good news that God will enable the Muslims to seize his forelock, so that they drag him to death if he returns to the prohibition. When he did return, God, exalted is He, undoubtedly enabled them to seize his forelock on the Day of Badr. It is reported that when the surah of Ar-Rahman was revealed, **"The Most Merciful taught the Qur'an"** (Ar-Rahman 2), the Prophet, peace be upon him, said to his companions: "Who among you will recite it to the chiefs of Quraysh?" They hesitated, fearing harm from them. Ibn Masʿud stood and said, "I will, O Messenger of God." He, peace be upon him, had him sit down, then said: "Who will recite it to them?" No one stood except Ibn Masʿud. Then a third time, and so on, until he was permitted. The Prophet, peace be upon him, had been holding him back, because he knew his weakness and the smallness of his body. Then he reached them and found them gathered around the Kaʿbah, and he began reciting the surah. Abu Jahl stood up and slapped him, splitting his ear and making it bleed. He departed with his eyes weeping. When the Prophet, peace be upon him, saw him, his heart softened and he lowered his head in grief. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, came laughing and rejoicing, and he said: "O Gabriel, you laugh while Ibn Masʿud weeps?" He said: "You will know." Then, when the Muslims prevailed on the Day of Badr, Ibn Masʿud sought to have a share among the fighters, and he began looking over the slain. He found Abu Jahl lying struck down, groaning. He feared that there might still be strength in him that could harm him, so he placed the spear on his nostril from a distance and stabbed him. Perhaps this is the meaning of His saying: **"We will brand him on the snout."** Then, when he realized his own inability and that he could not climb onto his chest due to his weakness, he ascended to him by a stratagem. When Abu Jahl saw him, he said: "O little shepherd (ruwayʿi al-ghanam), you have climbed a difficult height!" Ibn Masʿud said: "Islam rises and is not risen above." Abu Jahl said: "Tell your companion that no one was more hateful to me in my life, nor more hateful to me in the state of my death." It is reported that when the Prophet, peace be upon him, heard this, he said: "The Pharaoh of this nation is more severe than the Pharaoh of Moses, for he said **'I believe'** (Yunus 90), while this one has increased in arrogance." Then he said to Ibn Masʿud: "Cut off my head with this sword of mine, for it is sharper and keener." When he cut off his head, he could not lift it.

Perhaps the Wise, glorified is He, created him weak precisely so that he would not be able to lift it, for several reasons:

First: He is a dog, and a dog is dragged.

Second: Because of the splitting of his ear, so that the ear is repaid with an ear.

Third: To fulfill the threat mentioned in His saying **"We will surely seize him by the forelock"**, so that that head is dragged by its front part. Then, when Ibn Masʿud could not bear it, he split his ear, inserted the cord into it, and began dragging him toward the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, while Gabriel was before him laughing and saying: "O Muhammad, an ear for an ear, but the head is here along with the ear!"

This is what has been reported about the killing of Abu Jahl. I have transmitted it according to its meaning, not its wording. The sinner's (*al-khati'*) meaning of His saying **"We will surely seize him by the forelock."**

**The fourth matter:** The *nasiyah* is the hair of the forehead, and the place of the hair may also be called the *nasiyah*. God, exalted is He, here used the forelock as a metaphor for the face and head. Perhaps the reason is that Abu Jahl was very concerned with combing and perfuming that forelock, and perhaps he also took care to blacken it, so God, exalted is He, informed him that He would blacken it along with his face.

**The fifth matter:** God, exalted is He, defined the forelock with the definite article, as though He were saying: "The forelock known to you, its essence is known, but its attributes are unknown to you. A forelock, and what a forelock! Lying in speech and sinful in deed." He described it as lying only because its owner was lying against God, exalted is He, in claiming that He had not sent Muhammad, and lying against His Messenger in claiming that he was a sorcerer, a liar, or not a prophet. It was also said: his lying was his saying, "I am the greatest of the people of this valley in assemblies." He described the forelock as sinful because its owner rebels against God, exalted is He. God, exalted is He, said: **"None eats it except the sinners"** (Al-Haqqah 37). The difference between *khati'* and *mukhti'* is that the *khati'* is punished and held accountable, while the *mukhti'* is not held accountable. He described the forelock as sinful and lying, just as He described faces as looking, in His saying, exalted is He: **"Looking toward their Lord"** (Al-Qiyamah 23).

**The sixth matter:** *Nasiyatin* (a forelock) is a substitute (badal) for *al-nasiyah* (the forelock). It is permissible to substitute an indefinite noun for a definite one, because it has been qualified and thus has become independently meaningful.

**Seventh issue:** "Nasiyatun" (ناصِيَةٌ) was read in the nominative, with the implied sense "it is a forelock," and "nasiyatan" (ناصِيَةً) in the accusative. Both are in the sense of an object of vilification (shatm). Know that when the Messenger (ﷺ) spoke harshly to Abu Jahl and recited these verses to him, Abu Jahl said: "O Muhammad, whom are you threatening me with? I have the largest assembly in this valley." He boasted of his company, who used to eat up his plunder. So God the Exalted revealed: ﴿Then let him call his assembly﴾ ﴿We will call the guards of Hell﴾. In this there are several issues:

**First issue:** The meaning of "nadi" (assembly) was already explained at His words: ﴿and you commit the wrong in your assemblies﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:29]. Abu 'Ubayda said: "nadiyahu" means the people of his assembly. In general, the meaning of "nadi" is its people, and a place is not called a nadi unless its people are in it. It was called nadi because the people gather at it (yandduna ilayhi nadan wa nadwatan), and from this comes Dar al-Nadwa in Makkah, where they used to gather for consultation. It was also said that it was named nadi because it is a gathering of generosity and bounty, and this was mentioned in a sarcastic manner, meaning: gather the people of generosity and defence, as you claim, so that they may help you.

**Second issue:** Abu 'Ubayda and al-Mubarrad said: the singular of "al-zabaniyah" (the guards) is "zibniyah," and its root is from "zabantuhu," meaning "I pushed him," and it is one who is rebellious, whether human or jinn. Similar in meaning and form is "'ifriyah"; one says: "Fulan zibniyah 'ifriyah" (so-and-so is a fierce, stubborn one). Al-Akhfash said: some said its singular is "al-zabani," others said "al-zabin," and others said this is from the plural that has no singular from its own form in the Arabic language, like "ababil" and "'abadid." In general, what is meant is the angels of punishment, and there is no doubt that they are distinguished by great strength. Muqatil said: they are the keepers of Hell, whose feet are on the earth and whose heads are in the sky. Qatada said: "al-zabaniyah" in the speech of the Arabs means the police, and they are the harsh, severe angels; the angels of the Fire were named al-zabaniyah because they push the disbelievers (yazbinunahum), that is, they thrust them into Hell.

**Third issue:** Regarding the verse there are two opinions:

The first: meaning, let him do what he mentioned, that he calls his helpers and seeks their aid in opposing Muhammad. If he does that, then We will call the guards against whom neither he nor his people have any strength. Ibn 'Abbas said: if he called his assembly, the guards would seize him at once, visibly before them. It was also said: this is a report from God the Exalted that he will be dragged in this world like a dog, and this was indeed done to him on the day of Badr. And it was said: rather, this is a report that the guards will drag him in the Hereafter to the Fire.

The second opinion: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse, meaning: "We will surely seize him by the forelock" and "We will call the guards" in the Hereafter; then let him call his assembly at that time, and then let them prevent him.

**Fourth issue:** The "fa" (then) in His words ﴿Then let him call his assembly﴾ indicates the challenge (al-mu'jiz). This is because it is an incitement to the disbeliever to call upon his assembly and his people. Whenever the disbeliever does that, the calling of the guards follows from it. Since the disbeliever did not dare to do so, this shows the manifestation of the miracle (mu'jiz) of the Messenger (ﷺ).

**Fifth issue:** It was read "sa-tud'a" (passive). The letter "sin" here is not for doubt; rather, what comes from God is certain to occur, especially when the Messenger (ﷺ) was given the good news that He would avenge him upon his enemy. Perhaps the purpose of the "sin" is what is meant by the words of the Messenger (ﷺ): "Indeed I will surely support you, even if after a while."

Then He said: "Nay!" (kallā), which is a rebuke to Abu Jahl. It was also said: its meaning is that he will not reach what he boasts of, namely that he calls his assembly, "Let him call his assembly; We shall summon the guards of hell." (Even) if he calls them, they will not benefit him or help him. He is too humble and contemptible to oppose you. It is also possible that it means he will not attain what he desires of your obedience to him when he forbids you from prayer. And it was said: its meaning is, "Beware, do not obey him."

* * *
Then He said: "Do not obey him" (lā tuṭiʻhu), like His saying: "So do not obey the deniers" (Al-Qalam: 8). "And prostrate yourself" (wa-skjud). According to most of the people of interpretation (ta'wil), He meant by it: pray, and devote yourself to the worship of God, Exalted is He, through action and conveyance (of the message). Let your thought dwell little on this enemy, for God is your strengthener and helper. Some said: rather, the intended meaning is submission (khuḍūʻ). Others said: rather, the intended meaning is the prostration itself in prayer.

* * *
Then He said: "And draw near" (wa-qtarib). The intended meaning is: seek, through your prostration, nearness of rank to your Lord. In a hadith: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he prostrates." Some said: the intended meaning is, "Prostrate, O Muhammad, and draw near, O Abu Jahl, to Him, until you see what the seizing of the guards (al-zabaniyah) will inflict upon you." So it is as if God, Exalted is He, commanded him to prostrate in order that the disbeliever's rage might increase, like His saying: "That He may enrage the disbelievers by them" (Al-Fath: 29). The cause that makes his rage increase is that disbelief used to prevent him from standing (in prayer), so his rage and anger at witnessing the prostration are more complete. Then He said at that point: "And draw near" to Him, O Abu Jahl, and place your foot upon him, for the man is prostrate and occupied with himself. This is mockery of him and belittling of his station. And God, Glorified and Exalted, knows best. May God bless our master Muhammad, and his family and companions, and grant them peace.
